title: Baghdad and the golden age
blurb: Baghdad, Cordoba and Cairo lead the world in science, medicine and law. Crusaders and Mongols arrive. Baghdad burns.

events.title: Paper from China
events.what: Abbasid and Tang armies meet at Talas. Chinese prisoners bring paper-making to the Muslim world.

events.title: Al-Mansur secures the Abbasids
events.what: Al-Mansur succeeds his brother al-Saffah, puts down rivals and has the powerful general Abu Muslim killed. The centre of the caliphate moves from Syria to Iraq.
events.tie: Ruling from Iraq, the Abbasids drew Persian learning and Persian converts into the heart of the Muslim world.
events.note: In 750 most of the Umayyad family were massacred at Abu Futrus; Abd al-Rahman escaped to Spain.

events.title: Cordoba
events.what: The Umayyad prince who escaped the Abbasids founds an independent state in Cordoba. Its great mosque rises in 785.
events.tie: From Cordoba, Islam was taught and prayed in Spain for over seven centuries, and its Great Mosque became a school of Maliki law.

events.title: Baghdad is founded
events.what: Caliph al-Mansur founds Baghdad as a round city on the Tigris. Within fifty years it is the largest city on earth.
events.tie: Baghdad became a home of hadith, law and science; Imam Abu Hanifa is buried there and Imam Ahmad ibn Hanbal taught there.

events.title: The four imams
events.what: Abu Hanifa dies in Baghdad. Malik, al-Shafii and Ahmad follow over the next century. The four schools of law take shape.

events.title: Harun al-Rashid
events.what: Harun al-Rashid becomes caliph. The Baghdad of the Thousand and One Nights is at its peak.
events.tie: In Harun's Baghdad, Abu Yusuf, the student of Abu Hanifa, served as chief judge and wrote his book on taxation for the caliph.

events.title: Baghdad's paper mill
events.what: Baghdad's first paper mill opens under Harun al-Rashid. Cheap paper replaces papyrus and parchment, and bookshops fill a whole street.
events.tie: Copies of the Quran, once costly treasures written on skin, became affordable for ordinary families.
events.note: Paper-making came from China by way of Samarkand.

events.title: Charlemagne and Harun
events.what: Charlemagne is crowned emperor in the west. He exchanges gifts with Harun al-Rashid, including an elephant.
events.tie: Harun's envoys brought an elephant named Abul-Abbas and later a water clock, showing Europe the wealth and learning of the Muslim world.

events.title: The road of Zubaydah
events.what: Harun's wife Zubaydah builds wells and rest stops along the 1,400 km pilgrim road from Kufa to Makkah.

events.title: The book of al-jabr
events.what: Al-Khwarizmi writes his book on al-jabr, 'completion and balancing', which gives algebra its name. Much of it works out the inheritance shares set by the Quran.
events.note: His own name, Latinised, gave Europe the word 'algorithm'.
events.wiki: The Compendious Book on Calculation by Completion and Balancing

events.title: Muslims land in Sicily
events.what: The Aghlabids of Kairouan land in Sicily under the judge and scholar Asad ibn al-Furat. Palermo falls in 831 and is a Muslim city for two centuries.
events.tie: Asad had studied with Imam Malik in Madinah, so the law of Madinah crossed with him into Europe.
events.note: Asad died in 828 during the siege of Syracuse.

events.title: The House of Wisdom
events.what: Al-Mamun's House of Wisdom translates Greek, Persian and Indian science. Al-Khwarizmi writes the book that names algebra.

events.title: The Mihna
events.what: Al-Mamun orders judges and scholars to declare the Quran created. Ahmad ibn Hanbal refuses, is chained, jailed and flogged, and becomes a hero of the people.
events.note: The test went on under al-Mutasim and al-Wathiq and was ended by al-Mutawakkil around 848 to 851.

events.title: Samarra
events.what: Caliph al-Mutasim builds a new capital at Samarra for his Turkish slave guard. Al-Mutawakkil later raises its Great Mosque with a spiral minaret.
events.tie: Caliphs came to depend on slave soldiers, the road that later led to the Mamluks who stopped the Mongols.

events.title: Sahih al-Bukhari
events.what: Al-Bukhari completes his Sahih after sixteen years sifting 600,000 reports. Muslim ibn al-Hajjaj follows with his own.

events.title: Fatima al-Fihri's mosque
events.what: Fatima al-Fihri, a merchant's daughter from Kairouan, spends her inheritance on a mosque in Fez. Al-Qarawiyyin grows into a university that still teaches.
events.note: Her story is told by later chroniclers such as Ibn Abi Zar, and some details are debated.

events.title: The Zanj revolt
events.what: Enslaved East Africans forced to scrape the salt marshes of southern Iraq rise up. For fourteen years they hold the marshes, and they sack Basra.
events.note: Their leader, Ali ibn Muhammad, claimed descent from Ali; historians doubt it.

events.title: The Mosque of Ibn Tulun
events.what: Ahmad ibn Tulun, Egypt's governor, builds a vast mosque with a spiral minaret like Samarra's. It is the oldest mosque in Cairo still in its first form.
events.tie: Egypt now ran its own affairs while praying for the caliph, the first of many such dynasties along the Nile.

events.title: The Fatimids
events.what: The Shia Fatimids declare a rival caliphate in North Africa. In 969 they take Egypt and found Cairo.
events.tie: The Fatimids built al-Azhar in Cairo; after Salah al-Din restored Abbasid allegiance in 1171, it grew into the Muslim world's most famous university.

events.title: Al-Tabari
events.what: Al-Tabari dies, leaving the great early tafsir and a history of the world from creation to his own day.

events.title: The Caliphate of Cordoba
events.what: Abd al-Rahman III declares himself caliph. Cordoba has paved streets, street lights and a library of 400,000 books.
events.tie: The Quran's first command was 'Recite' (96:1), and under the caliphs Cordoba's libraries made it one of the great book cities of Islam.

events.title: The Black Stone is stolen
events.what: The Qarmatians storm Makkah during Hajj, kill pilgrims, throw bodies into Zamzam and carry the Black Stone off to eastern Arabia. It is returned in 951.
events.note: The stone came back after some 22 years (339 AH).

events.title: The Buyids take Baghdad
events.what: The Buyids, soldiers from the hills south of the Caspian, take Baghdad. The Abbasid caliph keeps his title but loses his power.
events.tie: For a century the caliph's name was still said in the Friday sermon while other men ruled.

events.title: Song China
events.what: The Song dynasty reunites China. Its ports fill with Arab and Persian merchants, who live in their own quarters with mosques and judges.
events.tie: Quanzhou's Qingjing Mosque, by its Arabic inscription founded in 1009, still stands from this trade.
events.note: Some historians date the Qingjing building later than its inscription.

events.title: Al-Azhar
events.what: Al-Azhar mosque opens in the new city of Cairo. It becomes one of the oldest universities still teaching.

events.title: Mahmud of Ghazna
events.what: Mahmud of Ghazna begins his campaigns into northern India. Lahore becomes a Muslim city.
events.tie: Under Ghaznavid rule the scholar al-Hujwiri, remembered as Data Ganj Bakhsh, settled in Lahore, and Islam spread through Punjab.

events.title: The Book of Optics
events.what: Kept under house arrest in Cairo, Ibn al-Haytham writes the Book of Optics. He shows that light enters the eye and tests every claim by experiment.
events.note: The story that he feigned madness to escape a task set by Caliph al-Hakim comes from later biographers. The book was written over roughly 1011 to 1021.

events.title: Ibn Sina and Ibn al-Haytham
events.what: Ibn Sina finishes the Canon of Medicine, Europe's textbook for 600 years. In Cairo, Ibn al-Haytham founds optics by experiment.

events.title: Al-Biruni's India
events.what: Al-Biruni, who travelled with Mahmud's armies, learns Sanskrit and writes a careful, fair study of India's religion, science and customs.
events.tie: It is one of the first works of comparative religion, in the spirit of 49:13: peoples made to know one another.

events.title: The Great Schism
events.what: The churches of Rome and Constantinople excommunicate each other. Christianity splits into a Catholic West and an Orthodox East.
events.tie: The Quran warns against splitting after clear proofs (3:105); the divided Christian world met the Seljuks seventeen years later at Manzikert.

events.title: The Seljuk Turks
events.what: The Seljuk Turks enter Baghdad as protectors of the caliph. Turkish dynasties will dominate the Muslim world for 900 years.
events.tie: The Seljuks built Nizamiyya madrasas across Iraq and Persia, where scholars like Imam al-Ghazali taught Sunni law and theology.

events.title: The Normans take Sicily
events.what: Norman knights under Roger I conquer Muslim Sicily, taking Palermo in 1072. Arab scholars, poets and craftsmen stay on at the Norman court.
events.tie: Through Sicily and Spain, Arabic science and books poured into Christian Europe.

events.title: The Nizamiyya colleges
events.what: The Seljuk vizier Nizam al-Mulk opens the Nizamiyya colleges. Al-Ghazali later teaches here.

events.title: Manzikert
events.what: Alp Arslan captures the Byzantine emperor at Manzikert. Anatolia opens to the Turks and becomes Turkey.

events.title: Ghana and the Almoravids
events.what: The Almoravids are said to take Koumbi Saleh, capital of Ghana. In 1068 al-Bakri had already described its Muslim town with twelve mosques.
events.tie: Gold caravans carried Islam across the Sahara, preparing the way for Mali.
events.note: Arab sources speak of a conquest; many historians now think Islam spread in Ghana mostly through trade and alliance.

events.title: Toledo falls
events.what: Alfonso VI of Castile takes Toledo from its quarrelling Muslim king. Its libraries make it Europe's centre for turning Arabic books into Latin.
events.tie: The feuding taifa kings lost Toledo, as the Quran warns: do not dispute, or you will lose courage and your strength will depart (8:46).

events.title: Kanem accepts Islam
events.what: Hummay, king of Kanem near Lake Chad, accepts Islam. Kanem, and later Bornu, remains a Muslim kingdom for some eight centuries.
events.tie: Islam reached Lake Chad by caravan and scholar, not by conquest.
events.note: The date comes from the royal chronicle (the Girgam). Some sources say an earlier king was Muslim.

events.title: Sagrajas
events.what: Called in by the taifa kings, Yusuf ibn Tashfin crosses from Morocco and crushes Alfonso VI at Sagrajas, al-Zallaqa. Al-Andalus is saved for four more centuries.
events.note: Al-Mutamid of Seville is reported to have said he would rather herd camels in Africa than pigs in Castile.

events.title: The Crusaders take Jerusalem
events.what: The First Crusade takes Jerusalem and massacres its Muslim and Jewish inhabitants. Crusader states last two centuries.

events.title: The Swahili coast
events.what: Muslim towns of stone line the East African coast from Mogadishu to Kilwa, trading gold and ivory across the ocean.
events.tie: Islam came to East Africa by sea with merchants, and Kiswahili is full of Arabic words, like 'kitabu' for book.

events.title: Al-Ghazali
events.what: Al-Ghazali dies. His Revival of the Religious Sciences joins law, theology and the inner life into one path.

events.title: Angkor Wat
events.what: King Suryavarman II builds Angkor Wat, the largest religious monument on earth, as a temple-mountain for the Hindu god Vishnu.
events.tie: The neighbouring Cham people later embraced Islam, and their descendants are Cambodia's Muslims today.

events.title: Nur al-Din
events.what: Nur al-Din unites Muslim Syria against the Crusaders, builds schools and hospitals, and orders a carved minbar for al-Aqsa that he will never see in place.
events.tie: His minbar stood in al-Aqsa for 782 years, until an arsonist burned it in 1969.
events.note: His father Zengi took Edessa in 1144, the first Crusader state to fall.

events.title: Al-Idrisi's map
events.what: Al-Idrisi completes a map of the known world for the Norman king of Sicily. Europe copies it for three centuries.

events.title: Salah al-Din at Hattin
events.what: Salah al-Din destroys the Crusader army at Hattin and retakes Jerusalem without a massacre.

events.title: Jerusalem is Muslim again
events.what: Salah al-Din enters Jerusalem on 27 Rajab, the night Muslims remember the Isra. Christians may leave by ransom, many poor are freed without it, and there is no massacre.
events.tie: Al-Aqsa, the end of the Night Journey (17:1), was in Muslim hands again after 88 years, and Nur al-Din's minbar was set inside it.

events.title: Salah al-Din and Richard
events.what: Richard the Lionheart takes Acre but never reaches Jerusalem. The Treaty of Jaffa leaves the city Muslim and open to Christian pilgrims.
events.note: Chroniclers say Salah al-Din sent fruit and snow to Richard when he fell ill.

events.title: Ibn Rushd
events.what: Ibn Rushd dies. His commentaries on Aristotle shape European universities for centuries.

events.title: Genghis Khan
events.what: Genghis Khan unites the Mongols. Within twenty years his armies destroy the cities of Central Asia and Persia.
events.tie: His grandson Hulagu sacked Baghdad in 1258, yet within decades many Mongol rulers had themselves become Muslims.

events.title: The Delhi Sultanate
events.what: The Delhi Sultanate begins. Muslim rule in northern India continues for six centuries.
events.tie: Under the sultans, scholars and Sufi masters like Nizamuddin Auliya taught in Delhi, and Islam took root among millions in South Asia.

events.title: Al-Andalus starts to fall
events.what: Christian kings break the Almohad army. Cordoba falls in 1236 and Seville in 1248. Only Granada remains Muslim.

events.title: Magna Carta
events.what: English barons force King John to seal Magna Carta, a charter that limits the king's power by law.
events.tie: Muslim jurists had long taught that rulers stand under the Sharia like anyone else, commanded to judge with justice (4:58).

events.title: The massacre at Otrar
events.what: The Khwarazm governor of Otrar kills a caravan of merchants sent by Genghis Khan, and the Shah has an envoy put to death. The Mongol storm follows.

events.title: The Mongols reach Islam
events.what: The Mongols sack Bukhara, Samarkand and Merv. Whole cities are emptied.

events.title: Sundiata founds Mali
events.what: Sundiata Keita defeats the Sosso king Sumanguru at Kirina and founds the empire of Mali on the upper Niger.
events.tie: His heirs made Mali a Muslim empire, and Mansa Musa's Hajj in 1324 astonished Cairo.
events.note: Sundiata's story comes from the oral epic of the griots. Whether he himself was Muslim is debated.

events.title: Mansurah and the Mamluks
events.what: The crusade of Louis IX is crushed at Mansurah and the French king is captured. Shajar al-Durr steers Egypt through the crisis, and the Mamluk sultanate is born.
events.note: Shajar al-Durr ruled briefly as sultan in her own name, one of very few women to do so in Islamic history.

events.title: Baghdad falls
events.what: The Mongols sack Baghdad, kill the caliph and throw the libraries into the Tigris. Five centuries of Abbasid rule end.
